GEN: Moses, by Jewish and Christian tradition.
Most scholars see several sources or layers (often labelled J, E, P) brought together during or after the Babylonian exile; others argue for more unified composition.
Traditions very old; final form c. 6th–5th century BC on the critical view.
Creation, the fall, the flood and Babel (1–11), then the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph (12–50). Its themes are covenant, promise and blessing to the nations.
EXO: Composite sources as with Genesis; the date and route of the exodus are debated (13th century BC is the most common estimate).
Final form c. 6th–5th century BC on the critical view.
Israel’s slavery in Egypt, the call of Moses, the plagues and Passover, the crossing of the sea, the covenant and Ten Commandments at Sinai, and the building of the tabernacle.
LEV: Generally assigned to the Priestly source and the Holiness Code (17–26).
Priestly material of uncertain age; final form exilic or post-exilic.
Sacrifice, priesthood, purity and the Day of Atonement (16): how a holy God dwells among his people. “Love your neighbour as yourself” (19:18).
NUM: Composite, with Priestly and older narrative material.
As for the rest of the Pentateuch.
Forty years in the wilderness: the census, rebellion and the spies, the bronze serpent, Balaam, and the generation that would enter the land.
DEU: Widely linked to the “book of the law” found under King Josiah (2 Kings 22, c. 622 BC) and to the Deuteronomistic History.
7th century BC core on the critical view, revised in exile.
Moses’ speeches on the plains of Moab renewing the covenant: the Shema (6:4–5), blessings and curses, and the death of Moses.
JOS: Part of the Deuteronomistic History; archaeology complicates a single swift conquest.
The crossing of the Jordan, Jericho, the conquest and division of Canaan among the tribes, and the covenant at Shechem (“As for me and my house…”, 24:15).
JDG: Deuteronomistic editing of older hero stories.
A cycle of sin, oppression, crying out and rescue under judges such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson: “In those days there was no king in Israel” (21:25).
RUT: Dated anywhere from the monarchy to after the exile.
A Moabite widow’s loyalty to Naomi and marriage to Boaz; Ruth becomes great-grandmother of David and appears in Matthew’s genealogy of Jesus.
1SA: Part of the Deuteronomistic History, using older court sources.
Samuel, the rise and fall of Saul, Israel’s first king, and the anointing of David and his flight from Saul.
2SA: The “Succession Narrative” (9–20) is often thought to be early court history.
David’s reign: Jerusalem as capital, God’s covenant promise of an everlasting dynasty (7), Bathsheba and Nathan, and Absalom’s revolt.
1KI: Deuteronomistic History, drawing on royal annals.
Solomon and the Temple, the division of the kingdom, and the prophet Elijah against Ahab and Jezebel.
2KI: Elisha, the fall of the northern kingdom to Assyria (722 BC), Hezekiah and Josiah’s reforms, and the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon (587/586 BC).
1CH: The work of a post-exilic “Chronicler”, using Samuel–Kings.
Genealogies from Adam, then David’s reign retold with emphasis on worship, the Levites and preparations for the Temple.
2CH: Solomon to the exile, focused on Judah, the Temple and repentance, ending with Cyrus’ decree allowing the return.
EZR: Linked with Nehemiah and often with Chronicles; the order of Ezra and Nehemiah is debated.
The return from Babylon, rebuilding of the Temple, and Ezra’s reading and teaching of the law.
NEH: Contains an authentic memoir; edited with Ezra.
Nehemiah rebuilds Jerusalem’s walls under opposition and leads covenant renewal.
EST: A Persian-period story; its historicity is debated.
Esther, a Jewish queen of Persia, saves her people from Haman’s plot: the origin of Purim. The Hebrew text never names God.
JOB: Moses, in the Talmud; otherwise unknown.
A poetic masterpiece framed by a prose tale.
A righteous man loses everything; his friends insist he must have sinned. God answers from the whirlwind. The great biblical book on innocent suffering.
PSA: David for many psalms; also Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses.
Collected over centuries; titles were added later.
150 prayers and songs in five books: praise, lament, thanksgiving, royal and wisdom psalms. The prayer book of Israel and the Church.
PRO: Collections from different periods, some echoing Egyptian wisdom.
“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7): practical wisdom for life, Lady Wisdom, and the capable wife (31).
ECC: Most date it late because of its language.
c. 3rd century BC on the critical view.
“Vanity of vanities”: a frank look at toil, death and meaning, concluding “Fear God and keep his commandments”.
SOL: Love poems between a woman and her beloved. Jewish and Christian interpreters read it of God and Israel, Christ and the Church, or the soul.
ISA: Isaiah son of Amoz (8th century BC).
Most scholars divide it: 1–39 (Isaiah), 40–55 (exile), 56–66 (after the return); others defend unity.
Judgment and hope: Immanuel (7:14), the child born (9:6), the servant who suffers for others (52:13–53:12), and new heavens and new earth.
JER: The Greek text is about one-eighth shorter and in a different order.
The prophet of Jerusalem’s fall, called to “pluck up and to plant”, who promised a new covenant written on the heart (31:31–34).
LAM: Five acrostic laments over ruined Jerusalem, with hope at the centre: “his mercies… are new every morning” (3:22–23).
EZE: Ezekiel, a priest among the exiles.
Largely accepted as his, with editing.
Visions of God’s glory leaving and returning to the Temple, the valley of dry bones (37), and a new heart and spirit.
DAN: Most scholars date the visions to the Maccabean crisis (c. 165 BC); traditional scholars defend a 6th-century date.
Stories of faithfulness in exile (the furnace, the lions’ den) and apocalyptic visions of kingdoms and “one like a son of man” (7:13).
HOS: Hosea’s marriage to unfaithful Gomer pictures God’s steadfast love for unfaithful Israel.
JOE: A locust plague as a sign of the Day of the Lord; the promise to pour out the Spirit on all flesh (2:28), quoted at Pentecost.
AMO: “Let justice roll down like waters” (5:24): judgment on Israel’s injustice amid prosperity.
OBA: The shortest Old Testament book: judgment on Edom for gloating over Jerusalem’s fall.
JON: Many read it as a didactic story.
A reluctant prophet, a great fish, and God’s mercy to Nineveh. Jesus speaks of “the sign of Jonah”.
MIC: Judgment and hope; a ruler from Bethlehem (5:2); “do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with your God” (6:8).
NAH: A poem celebrating the coming fall of Nineveh, Assyria’s capital.
HAB: A prophet questions God about injustice; “the righteous shall live by his faith” (2:4), key for Paul and Luther.
ZEP: The Day of the Lord (the source of the hymn “Dies irae”) and the joy of restored Zion.
HAG: A call to rebuild the Temple after the return from exile.
ZEC: 9–14 are often attributed to a later hand.
Night visions, and a humble king riding on a donkey (9:9), “they shall look on him whom they have pierced” (12:10).
MAL: Possibly a title rather than a name.
Disputes with priests and people; the messenger who prepares the way and the return of Elijah (4:5), the last words of the Christian Old Testament.
MAT: Most scholars think it used Mark and a sayings source (“Q”); author unknown.
c. 80–90 on the majority view; earlier on the traditional view.
Jesus as the Messiah who fulfils Israel’s scriptures: five great discourses including the Sermon on the Mount, ending with the Great Commission.
MAR: Widely held to be the earliest Gospel.
A fast-moving account of Jesus’ deeds, the hidden Messiah, and the cross, ending at the empty tomb (16:8; the longer ending is absent in the oldest manuscripts).
LUK: Same author as Acts; date debated.
c. 80–90 on the majority view; 60s on the traditional view.
An “orderly account” of Jesus’ life with the infancy narratives, parables like the Prodigal Son and Good Samaritan, and concern for the poor and outsiders.
JOH: The apostle John, “the disciple whom Jesus loved”.
Many scholars see a Johannine community and stages of composition.
The Word made flesh: seven signs, the “I am” sayings, the farewell discourses, and the glory of the cross. The great source of later Christology.
ACT: Historical reliability debated in detail; author accepted as the same as Luke.
From the Ascension and Pentecost to Paul in Rome: the spread of the Church “to the end of the earth” and the Council of Jerusalem (15).
ROM: Paul’s fullest statement of the gospel: sin, justification by faith, life in the Spirit, Israel and the nations, and Christian living.
1CO: Answers to a divided church: factions, morality, marriage, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts, the hymn to love (13), and the resurrection (15).
2CO: Undisputed, though many think it combines several letters.
Paul defends his ministry: strength in weakness, the new covenant, reconciliation, and the collection for Jerusalem.
GAL: Against requiring circumcision of Gentiles: justification by faith, freedom in Christ, and the fruit of the Spirit.
EPH: Many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name.
The Church as Christ’s body, salvation by grace through faith (2:8), unity, and the armour of God.
PHI: Joy in suffering and the hymn to Christ who emptied himself (2:5–11).
COL: Christ the image of the invisible God, firstborn of creation (1:15–20), against a false philosophy.
1TH: c. 50: probably the earliest New Testament writing.
Encouragement to a young church and teaching on the Lord’s coming.
2TH: Corrects the idea that the Day of the Lord had already come.
1TI: Most scholars consider the Pastoral Epistles later and pseudonymous; traditional scholars defend Paul.
Church order: bishops/overseers and deacons, sound teaching, and the Church as “pillar and bulwark of the truth” (3:15).
2TI: Paul’s farewell: “I have fought the good fight” (4:7), and “all Scripture is inspired by God” (3:16).
TIT: Appointing elders in Crete and the grace of God that trains believers.
PHM: A personal letter asking Philemon to receive his runaway slave Onesimus “as a beloved brother”.
HEB: Paul, in Eastern tradition; doubted in the early West.
Author unknown (Barnabas, Apollos and others proposed); Origen: “who wrote it, God knows”.
Christ greater than angels, Moses and the priesthood; the once-for-all sacrifice; the great chapter of faith (11).
JAM: James the brother of the Lord.
Some think pseudonymous; others accept James.
Practical faith: “faith without works is dead” (2:26). Luther called it “an epistle of straw” compared with Paul.
1PE: Hope for suffering Christians: a royal priesthood (2:9), and Christ who preached to the spirits in prison (3:19).
2PE: Widely regarded as pseudonymous and among the latest NT writings; doubted in antiquity too.
Against false teachers and scoffers about the Lord’s return; “partakers of the divine nature” (1:4).
1JO: “God is love” (4:8): tests of true faith against those who denied Christ had come in the flesh.
2JO: A short letter to “the elect lady” on truth and love.
3JO: A note to Gaius about hospitality and the troublesome Diotrephes.
JUD: A warning against false teachers, quoting 1 Enoch.
REV: John, exiled on Patmos; traditionally the apostle.
Dionysius of Alexandria (3rd c.) already argued it was a different John; reception slow in the East.
Letters to seven churches and visions of the Lamb, conflict with evil, and the new Jerusalem. Read in preterist, historicist, futurist and symbolic ways.
TOB: A Jewish story of the diaspora; Aramaic and Hebrew fragments found at Qumran.
Tobit’s blindness, his son Tobias’ journey with the angel Raphael, and marriage to Sarah: almsgiving, prayer and providence.
JDT: The widow Judith saves her city by beheading the general Holofernes.
ESG: Six Greek additions that bring God and prayer into the story.
Esther in the Greek form read by Catholics and Orthodox, including Mordecai’s dream and the prayers of Mordecai and Esther.
WIS: Written in Greek by an Alexandrian Jew.
Wisdom as “a breath of the power of God” (7:25), the immortality of the righteous soul, and God’s acts in the exodus. Echoed in Hebrews 1:3.
SIR: Jesus son of Sirach, translated by his grandson.
Hebrew manuscripts survive in large part (Cairo Geniza, Masada).
A long book of wisdom on daily life, the law, and praise of “famous men” (44–50). Also called Ecclesiasticus, “the church book”.
BAR: Confession, wisdom identified with the law, and comfort for Jerusalem. Chapter 6 in Catholic Bibles is the Letter of Jeremiah.
EPJ: A satire against idols, addressed to the exiles.
1MA: The revolt of the Maccabees against Antiochus IV, the rededication of the Temple (the origin of Hanukkah), and the Hasmonean leaders.
2MA: The martyrdom of Eleazar and the seven brothers, resurrection hope, and prayer for the dead (12:42–46).
1ES: Josiah to Ezra, with the contest of the three guards (“truth is great and prevails”).
4ES: A Jewish apocalypse with Christian additions.
Visions after the fall of Jerusalem in 70, wrestling with suffering and justice. In the Vulgate appendix and Anglican Apocrypha.
PRM: A short, moving prayer of repentance.
PSX: A Hebrew form was found at Qumran.
David’s psalm about his anointing and his victory over Goliath; in Orthodox Bibles at the end of the Psalter.
PRA: The prayer of Azariah and the hymn of the three young men in the furnace (“Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord”), sung in Christian morning prayer.
SUS: Young Daniel exposes the false witnesses against the faithful Susanna.
BEL: Daniel exposes the priests of the idol Bel and kills a dragon worshipped in Babylon.
3MA: A Greek Jewish story; not about the Maccabees.
Ptolemy IV’s persecution of the Jews of Egypt and their deliverance.
4MA: Devout reason is master of the passions, shown through the Maccabean martyrs.
DNG: Daniel in the Greek form, including the Song of the Three, Susanna, and Bel and the Dragon.

trad: Christ builds the Church on Peter personally; the keys and the power to bind and loose pass to his successors, the bishops of Rome (Vatican I, Pastor aeternus).
Peter is first among the apostles, and the rock is often read as his confession of faith shared by every faithful bishop; it does not give Rome jurisdiction over the whole Church.
Most read the rock as Peter’s confession of Christ or as Christ himself (cf. 1 Corinthians 3:11); some accept a role for Peter personally, but deny that it passes to a papal office.
Fathers read it in several ways: Cyprian of Peter as the source of unity; Augustine often of Peter’s confession; Leo the Great of Peter living on in his see.
Eating the flesh of the Son of Man
Refers to the Eucharist, in which bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation, Trent 1551).
Refers to the Eucharist, the true body and blood of Christ; the change is affirmed as a mystery without a philosophical definition.

Lutherans: Christ’s body is truly present “in, with and under” the bread. Reformed: a real spiritual feeding by faith. Zwinglians and many evangelicals: eating means believing, and the passage is not about the Supper.
Early writers such as Ignatius (c. 110) and Justin (c. 150) already speak of the Eucharist as the flesh of Jesus.
Justified by faith apart from works of the law

Initial justification is a free gift received by faith without prior merit; “works of the law” are the Mosaic law. Justification also renews the person inwardly, and grace bears fruit in good works (Trent, session 6).
Salvation is theosis: union with God by grace, received in faith and lived in the sacraments and ascetic struggle. The forensic framing of the Western debate is often thought too narrow.
Justification is God’s declaration that the sinner is righteous through faith alone (sola fide), by Christ’s righteousness imputed; works follow as fruit, not as ground.
The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), signed by Catholics and Lutherans and later by Methodists, Reformed and Anglicans, states a common understanding of basic truths.
Justified by works and not by faith alone
Confirms that faith working through love, not faith alone, justifies; good works done in grace increase justification.
Faith and works are inseparable in the life of grace; the verse is read with Paul, not against him.
James speaks of showing or demonstrating justification before others, or of a dead, merely intellectual “faith”; living faith always produces works.
Luther placed James at the back of his New Testament and called it “an epistle of straw” beside Paul, while still reading and preaching it.
The Church, pillar and bulwark of the truth
The Church, through the bishops in communion with the pope, is the authoritative guardian and interpreter of revealed truth.
The Church as a whole, guided by the Holy Spirit and expressed in the councils and the consensus of the Fathers, guards the truth.
The Church upholds and proclaims the truth of Scripture; Scripture remains the final authority over the Church (sola scriptura).
The words of institution effect the change of the bread and wine; the Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary.
The change is completed in the whole anaphora, especially the epiclesis calling down the Spirit; the Liturgy is the bloodless sacrifice.
At Marburg (1529) Luther insisted on “is”; Zwingli read “signifies”. Calvin taught a real spiritual presence. Most Protestants reject the Mass as a sacrifice.
Institutes the sacrament of penance: priests absolve sins in Christ’s name.
The basis of the mystery of confession; the priest is witness and the absolution is prayed in Christ’s name.
Usually read as the authority to proclaim forgiveness through the gospel; Lutherans and Anglicans keep private confession and absolution as an option.
Kecharitōmenē, “having been graced”, supports Mary’s fullness of grace, read as part of the basis for the Immaculate Conception (1854).
Mary is honoured as Theotokos and all-holy, but the Immaculate Conception is generally not accepted, since it is tied to a Western view of original sin.
Many translate “favoured one”: Mary is a model believer chosen by grace, without additional doctrines about her.
“Until” does not imply what happened afterwards; Mary remained ever-virgin, and the “brothers” of Jesus were relatives.
Mary is ever-virgin; the brothers are usually explained as Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage.
The Reformers (Luther, Calvin, Zwingli) mostly held Mary’s perpetual virginity; most Protestants today read the brothers as later children of Mary and Joseph.
Jerome argued the brothers were cousins; Epiphanius that they were Joseph’s sons; Helvidius (c. 383) that they were Mary’s.
Supports praying and offering the Mass for the dead and the doctrine of purgatory.
Supports prayer for the departed, practised in every memorial service, without the Western doctrine of purgatory.
The book is not canonical; most Protestants reject prayer for the dead, although some Anglicans and Lutherans keep forms of it.
Often cited, with other texts, for purgatory: a purification after death for those who die in grace.
Read as the testing of a teacher’s work; the departed are helped by prayer, but purgatory as a place of satisfaction is rejected.
The Day of judgment tests the quality of each minister’s work; not a doctrine of purgatory.
The Spirit who proceeds from the Father
The Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son (Filioque) as from one principle; the Father is the source within the Trinity.
The Spirit proceeds from the Father alone; the Son sends the Spirit in time. The Latin addition of “and the Son” to the creed is a key cause of the schism.
Western Protestants generally kept the Filioque; several Anglican and Lutheran bodies now allow the creed without it.
Scripture and apostolic Tradition together form one deposit of faith, interpreted by the Magisterium (Dei Verbum).
Holy Tradition is the life of the Spirit in the Church, of which Scripture is the heart.
The apostles’ teaching, oral or written, is now preserved in Scripture, the sole infallible rule; later traditions are tested by it.
All Scripture is inspired by God
Affirms inspiration and inerrancy of Scripture, which is read within Tradition.
Scripture is God-breathed and read within the Church’s worship and the Fathers.
The central text for the sufficiency and supreme authority of Scripture.
The sacrament of the anointing of the sick (formerly extreme unction).
The mystery of holy unction, served for healing of soul and body.
Some practise anointing with prayer; not a sacrament for most.
Mercy on whom I will have mercy
God’s grace is entirely prior and free; predestination does not cancel human freedom (Thomist and Molinist views both allowed).
God foreknows but does not override freedom; salvation is synergy of grace and free response.
Calvinists: unconditional election (Dort). Arminians and Wesleyans: election based on foreseen faith, with prevenient grace for all. Lutherans: election to salvation without double predestination.
A valid sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved; the exception is read as unlawful unions. Annulment declares there was no valid marriage.
Marriage is indissoluble in principle, but the Church may permit a second (and third) marriage by economy, with a penitential rite.
Most allow divorce for adultery and often desertion (Westminster Confession 24), and remarriage.
One mediator between God and men
Christ is the sole mediator; the prayers of the saints share in his mediation, as believers on earth pray for one another.
The same: the saints’ intercession flows from Christ’s, and they are asked to pray for us.
Christ alone mediates; invoking saints is generally rejected, though asking fellow believers to pray is encouraged.
Forbids idolatry; images of Christ and the saints are permitted since the Incarnation, and veneration passes to the one depicted (Nicaea II).
The Incarnation makes the icon possible; icons are venerated, not worshipped (the Triumph of Orthodoxy, 843).
Lutherans keep images; Reformed churches counted this as a separate (second) commandment and removed images from worship.
Catholics and Lutherans follow Augustine’s numbering, joining this to the first commandment; Orthodox and Reformed count it separately.
Prophecy of the virgin birth, as Matthew 1:23 reads it.
The same; the Septuagint parthenos (“virgin”) is the Church’s text.
Traditional Protestants read it as messianic prophecy; many modern scholars note the Hebrew ‘almah means “young woman” and see a first fulfilment in Isaiah’s day.
The debate is old: Justin Martyr argued it with Trypho the Jew around 155.
The woman’s offspring will crush the serpent
The “Protoevangelium”: the first promise of the Redeemer. The Vulgate’s “she shall crush” (ipsa) shaped Marian art.
The first gospel promise, fulfilled in Christ born of the Virgin.
The first gospel promise of Christ’s victory; the Hebrew pronoun is masculine (“he” or “it”).

maps.note: Ur is usually identified with Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq; some scholars prefer a northern Ur near Harran.
The route shown is the traditional one, with Sinai at Jebel Musa; the crossing point and the location of Sinai are debated.
Approximate tribal territories; the Levites received cities rather than a territory. Dan later moved north.
Sites as identified by long tradition; Tabor for the Transfiguration and Bethany beyond the Jordan are traditional identifications.
With Silas, then Timothy and Luke, c. 49–52.
c. 53–57, including over two years in Ephesus.
As a prisoner, c. 59–60, with shipwreck on Malta.
